slides.headline: Gardening without the Monday back
slides.sub: Enjoy the weekend garden and still move well come Monday.

slides.title: Warm up like it's sport
slides.body: Gardening is a genuine workout. A five-minute walk around the yard, a few squats and some gentle trunk turns get your body ready before the first bag of soil.

slides.title: Kneel, don't stoop
slides.body: Long periods bent over from the waist are a common cause of stiffness. Kneel on a pad, sit on a low stool, or use long-handled tools for weeding and planting.

slides.title: Switch jobs every 20 minutes
slides.body: Rotate between weeding, pruning, raking and carrying so no single position lasts too long. Stand up, lean back gently and walk for a minute between jobs.

slides.title: Lift close, turn with your feet
slides.body: Keep bags and pots close to your body, bend at your knees and hips, and turn with your feet rather than twisting. Use a wheelbarrow or split heavy loads in two.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain spreading down a leg, numbness, weakness, or changes to bladder or bowel control need prompt medical attention. Stiffness that hasn't eased after a week or two is worth assessing.

slides.headline: Back in the garden, comfortably
slides.body: Our chiropractors assess how you move, then combine hands-on care and exercise to help you stay active outdoors. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Spring garden plans? Your back would like a say. 🌱

Gardening is real physical work, so treat it that way. Warm up with a short walk and a few squats, kneel or use a low stool instead of stooping for long periods, and switch jobs every 20 minutes or so.

When lifting bags of soil or pots, keep them close, bend at the hips and knees and turn with your feet. A wheelbarrow is your friend. Some stiffness the next day is common, but pain down a leg, numbness or weakness need prompt attention.
